stimuli.title: Corporate venture capital
stimuli.text:
Large companies have long invested in young firms, but the motives behind these investments differ from those of independent venture capitalists. An independent fund succeeds only if its investments return more cash than they cost, usually within about a decade. A corporate venture arm, by contrast, often accepts a lower financial return in exchange for a strategic benefit: an early look at a technology that could reshape the parent company's market.

This strategic motive has a cost that researchers have only recently measured. Startups backed by corporate investors tend to be valued more highly at each funding round, which looks like good news for founders. Yet several studies find that these startups are somewhat less likely to be acquired by a company other than their corporate backer. Rival buyers, it seems, hesitate to bid for a firm whose investor may already know its secrets or may hold the right to match any offer.

Some founders respond by limiting what a corporate investor may see, refusing it a board seat or keeping key technical data out of its reach. Such limits protect a startup's options, but they also weaken the very relationship that made the corporate investor attractive, since much of the value a large company offers, such as access to its distribution network or its engineers, depends on close cooperation. The choice of investor, in short, is less a question of who offers the most money than of which future the founders want to keep open.

stimuli.title: The honeybee waggle dance
stimuli.text:
For decades, biologists treated the honeybee waggle dance as a precise map. A forager returning to the hive runs a straight line whose angle from vertical gives the direction of a food source relative to the sun, and whose duration signals its distance. Recruits that follow the dance then fly out and, in principle, find the food.

Field experiments have complicated this picture. When researchers disrupted dances by turning hives on their sides, so that dancers could not orient their runs, colonies in some landscapes gathered almost as much food as normal colonies. In landscapes where food was patchy and scarce, however, the disrupted colonies did markedly worse. The dance, it appears, matters most when good food is hard to find; in rich landscapes, recruits can do nearly as well by relying on scent and on their own searching.

These findings do not mean the dance is a poor signal. Measurements show that individual dances are noisy, with successive runs pointing in slightly different directions, and that recruits often need several trips to locate a source. A colony, though, averages over many dancers and many recruits, so imprecise individual messages still steer the colony's foraging effort as a whole toward its richest patches.

stimuli.title: Default options in retirement saving
stimuli.text:
When employers enroll workers in a retirement plan automatically, letting them opt out rather than requiring them to sign up, participation rises sharply, in some firms from under half of new hires to over 90 percent. Economists in the behavioral tradition took this as evidence that many workers want to save but fail to act, and that a well-chosen default can help them do what they would choose with more time and attention.

Later work added a complication. Automatically enrolled workers tended to stay at the default contribution rate, often a modest 3 percent of pay, even though many of them would previously have chosen a higher rate on their own. Some ended up saving less than they would have under the old system. The default, it turned out, set not only whether people saved but how much.

Plan designers have since experimented with automatic escalation, in which contributions rise by a percentage point each year until they reach a higher ceiling. Early results suggest that most workers accept the increases as readily as they accepted enrollment. If so, the lesson of the first studies needs restating: defaults do not simply rescue people from inaction; they carry the designer's judgment about what people should do, which makes choosing them a responsibility rather than a technicality.

stimuli.title: Printing and English spelling
stimuli.text:
It is often said that the printing press fixed English spelling. The claim is half right. Printers did spread uniform spellings faster than scribes ever could, but for more than a century after the first English presses opened in the 1470s, spelling in printed books remained strikingly loose. The same compositor might set a word two ways on one page, and some did so on purpose: before printers took up the practice of widening the spaces between words to fill out a line, adding or dropping a letter was a convenient way to make each line reach the right margin.

What finally narrowed the variation was less the press itself than the people and institutions around it. Schoolmasters published spelling books that were widely used in teaching; dictionary makers, culminating in Samuel Johnson in 1755, offered word lists that printers could treat as authorities; and large printing houses issued house rules so that work done by many hands would look consistent. The press made a fixed spelling possible, and it made inconsistency more visible, but the decision to fix spelling was a social one.

stimuli.title: Dynamic pricing and fairness
stimuli.text:
Economists generally welcome dynamic pricing, in which a seller adjusts prices as demand changes. Higher prices at peak times ration scarce capacity toward the buyers who value it most, and they give sellers a reason to add capacity when it is most needed. Yet customers often react to price increases during a surge with anger that seems out of proportion to the sums involved, and firms that ignore this reaction can pay heavily.

Research on perceived fairness helps explain the anger. People tend to judge a price against a reference point, usually the price they are used to paying, and they accept increases that seem to reflect a seller's higher costs far more readily than increases that seem to exploit a buyer's urgent need. A snow shovel that costs more after a storm violates this norm, since the shop's costs have not changed; a shovel that costs more because steel prices rose does not.

Firms have learned to work around the norm rather than against it. Some present the normal price as the peak price and offer discounts in quiet periods, which shifts the reference point. Others tie surges to visible costs, such as paying drivers more to come out in bad weather. Neither tactic changes the economics of dynamic pricing, but each changes how customers read it.

stimuli.title: Finding planets by transit
stimuli.text:
Most of the planets known outside our solar system were found by the transit method: a telescope watches thousands of stars at once and records the slight, regular dimming that occurs when a planet passes in front of its star. The method has been remarkably productive, but it sees the galaxy through a narrow window. A transit can be observed only when a planet's orbit is aligned almost edge-on to our line of sight, and the closer a planet orbits its star, the more likely that alignment is. A planet orbiting close in also transits more often, so a short survey can catch several passes and confirm the signal.

As a result, early catalogs were crowded with large planets on tight orbits, and some astronomers briefly concluded that such planets were common. Statistical corrections have since reversed much of that impression. Once the odds of detection are accounted for, close-orbiting giant planets turn out to be rare, accompanying perhaps one star in a hundred, while smaller planets on wider orbits are far more numerous than the raw counts suggest. The lesson extends beyond astronomy: a sample tells us about the world only after we understand how the sample was drawn.

stimuli.title: Reviving a language
stimuli.text:
Efforts to revive endangered languages have often begun with documentation: linguists record the last fluent speakers, write grammars and compile dictionaries. Such work preserves a language for scholars, but it rarely produces new speakers. A language survives only if children acquire it, and children acquire languages they hear used for real purposes, not languages they meet in archives.

The revival of Hawaiian illustrates the difference. By the 1980s, fewer than fifty children spoke the language. Parents and teachers then founded preschools in which caregivers used only Hawaiian, followed by immersion schools in which the whole curriculum was taught in it. Since then thousands of students have been educated in Hawaiian, and a generation of parents is raising children who hear it at home.

The immersion model is demanding. It requires teachers fluent enough to teach mathematics or science in the language, along with books and technical terms that may not yet exist. Documentation, far from being made obsolete, becomes indispensable at this stage, since the grammars and recordings that once served only scholars now supply the raw material from which teachers build lessons.

stimuli.title: The paint tube and Impressionism
stimuli.text:
Accounts of Impressionism often credit a humble invention, the collapsible metal paint tube, introduced in the 1840s. Before it, painters stored ground pigment mixed with oil in pig bladders that leaked and dried out, which made sustained work outdoors awkward. The tube kept paint fresh and portable, and Renoir is reported to have said that without it there would have been no Impressionism.

Such remarks deserve some skepticism. Painters had sketched outdoors in oils long before the tube, and many Impressionist canvases that look spontaneous were finished, or painted entirely, in the studio. Yet the tube mattered in a less obvious way. The manufacturers who sold paint in tubes also sold new, intense pigments, such as cobalt violet and synthetic ultramarine, ready-mixed and consistent from one tube to the next. Painters could therefore lay bright colors directly on the canvas without first grinding and mixing them, a practice that helps account for the high-keyed palette the movement is known for.

stimuli.title: Network effects
stimuli.text:
A platform such as a ride-hailing app or an online marketplace becomes more valuable to each user as more users join, since buyers attract sellers and sellers attract buyers. This network effect is often said to produce winner-take-all markets: once one platform leads, newcomers cannot match its value, and the leader's position becomes unassailable.

The history of such markets is less tidy. Several once-dominant platforms lost their lead within a few years, among them early social networks and, in some countries, online auction sites. Two features help explain why network effects protect some leaders and not others. The first is multihoming: if users can easily use several platforms at once, as many drivers and riders do with competing ride-hailing apps, a newcomer need not pull users away from the leader to attract them. The second is locality. A ride-hailing network is valuable only within a city, so a rival can win one city at a time, whereas a messaging network that connects people across the world offers a newcomer no such foothold.

Network effects, then, raise the cost of entry, but whether they lock up a market depends on how users behave and on how far the network's value extends.

stimuli.title: Coral heat tolerance
stimuli.text:
Corals bleach when water that is too warm causes them to expel the algae living in their tissues, which supply most of their food. A coral that stays bleached for long starves. For years it was assumed that each coral species had a fixed heat tolerance, so that a given amount of warming would kill reefs in a predictable way.

Surveys after recent marine heat waves suggest more flexibility. Corals of a single species on reefs that regularly experience brief spikes in temperature often survive heat that kills the same species on steadier reefs. Experiments point to two sources of this tolerance: some corals host strains of algae that cope better with heat, and corals exposed to moderate stress appear to adjust their own cellular responses.

The finding is hopeful but limited. Tolerance gained in these ways raises the temperature a coral can survive by perhaps one degree Celsius, while the warming projected for many reefs this century is larger. Flexibility may buy reefs time; it does not make them safe.

stimuli.title: Lumen lamp launch
stimuli.text:
**Email from the marketing director**

We plan to launch the Lumen desk lamp in three markets in March. Based on our pilot, we expect first-year sales of 18,000 units in Market A, 12,000 units in Market B and 9,000 units in Market C. We will spend \$4 on advertising for each expected unit in each market.

**Cost sheet (per unit)**

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Retail price | \$60 |
| Retailer margin | 30% of retail price |
| Manufacturing | \$22 |
| Shipping to Market A | \$3 |
| Shipping to Market B | \$4 |
| Shipping to Market C | \$6 |

**Note from finance**

The board approves a launch in a market only if the expected first-year contribution in that market, after advertising, is at least \$150,000. Contribution per unit is the retail price minus the retailer margin, manufacturing and shipping.

stimuli.title: Warehouse supervisor hiring
stimuli.text:

questions.stem: A store raises the price of a jacket by 20 percent and later lowers the new price by 25 percent. The final price is what percent of the original price?
questions.explanation: Multiply the factors: $1.2 \times 0.75 = 0.9$, so the final price is 90 percent of the original. The changes do not cancel because the 25 percent cut is taken from a larger number.

questions.stem: If $\frac{x+3}{2} = \frac{2x-1}{3}$, what is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: Cross-multiply: $3(x+3) = 2(2x-1)$, so $3x + 9 = 4x - 2$ and $x = 11$.

questions.stem: If $n$ is a positive integer and $n^2$ is divisible by 72, what is the least possible value of $n$?
questions.explanation: $72 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2$. For $n^2$ to contain $2^3$, $n$ needs at least $2^2$ (since $n^2$ then has $2^4$); for $3^2$, $n$ needs one 3. The least $n$ is $2^2 \cdot 3 = 12$. Check: $144 / 72 = 2$.

questions.stem: If $2^x \cdot 4^{x+1} = 2^{11}$, what is the value of $x$?

In a class, the ratio of first-year to second-year students is 3 to 5. After 6 more first-year students join and no one leaves, the ratio becomes 3 to 4. How many second-year students are in the class?
questions.explanation: Let the counts be $3k$ and $5k$. Then $\frac{3k+6}{5k} = \frac{3}{4}$, so $12k + 24 = 15k$ and $k = 8$. Second-year students: $5 \cdot 8 = 40$.

questions.stem: A theater sold 40 tickets for a total of \$380. Adult tickets cost \$12 and child tickets cost \$7. How many adult tickets were sold?
questions.explanation: With $a$ adult tickets, $12a + 7(40 - a) = 380$, so $5a + 280 = 380$ and $a = 20$.

questions.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) of five numbers is 18. When one of the numbers is removed, the average of the remaining four numbers is 16. What number was removed?
questions.explanation: The five numbers sum to $5 \cdot 18 = 90$ and the four to $4 \cdot 16 = 64$. The removed number is $90 - 64 = 26$.

questions.stem: If $r$ and $s$ are the two solutions of $x^2 - 5x - 14 = 0$, what is the value of $r^2 + s^2$?
questions.explanation: Factor: $(x - 7)(x + 2) = 0$, so the solutions are 7 and $-2$. Then $49 + 4 = 53$. (Or use $r^2 + s^2 = (r+s)^2 - 2rs = 25 + 28 = 53$.)

questions.stem: Working alone at a constant rate, machine A makes 120 parts in 4 hours. Machine B, also at a constant rate, makes 120 parts in 6 hours. Working together, how many hours will the two machines take to make 300 parts?
questions.explanation: A makes 30 parts an hour and B makes 20, so together they make 50 an hour. $300 / 50 = 6$ hours.

questions.stem: How many integers $x$ satisfy $-3 < 2x + 5 \le 9$?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5: $-8 < 2x \le 4$. Divide by 2: $-4 < x \le 2$. The integers are $-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2$: six of them.

questions.stem: How many three-digit positive integers have only odd digits?
questions.explanation: Each of the three places can be 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9, so there are $5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125$ such integers.

questions.stem: What is the sum of all values of $x$ for which $|x - 4| = 2x + 1$?
questions.explanation: If $x - 4 = 2x + 1$, then $x = -5$, but then $2x + 1 = -9$, which cannot equal an absolute value, so reject it. If $4 - x = 2x + 1$, then $x = 1$, and $|1 - 4| = 3 = 2(1) + 1$. The only solution is 1, so the sum is 1.

questions.stem: A bag holds 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are blue?
questions.explanation: $\frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9} = \frac{30}{90} = \frac{1}{3}$. The answer $\frac{9}{25}$ would be right only with replacement.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = 2x^2 - 3$, what is the value of $f(f(1))$?
When the positive integer $k$ is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when $5k$ is divided by 6?
questions.explanation: Write $k = 6q + 4$. Then $5k = 30q + 20 = 6(5q + 3) + 2$, so the remainder is 2. A quick check: $k = 4$ gives $5k = 20$, remainder 2.

questions.stem: A delivery van travels 90 miles to a depot at 45 miles per hour and returns along the same road at 30 miles per hour. What is the average speed, in miles per hour, for the whole trip?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time: $\frac{180}{2 + 3} = 36$. Averaging 45 and 30 to get 37.5 ignores that more time is spent at the slower speed.

questions.stem: An investment of \$5,000 earns 4 percent annual interest, compounded annually. To the nearest dollar, what is it worth after 2 years?
questions.explanation: $5{,}000 \times 1.04^2 = 5{,}000 \times 1.0816 = 5{,}408$. Simple interest would give \$5,400; compounding adds interest on the first year's \$200.

questions.stem: In a sequence, $a_1 = 3$ and each term after the first is 2 more than twice the term before it. What is $a_4$?
What is the value of $\sqrt{50} + \sqrt{18}$?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2}$, so the sum is $8\sqrt{2}$. Roots of a sum do not combine as $\sqrt{68}$.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{3}{4}$ and $b \ne 0$, what is the value of $\frac{2a + b}{a - 2b}$?
questions.explanation: Any pair in the ratio works, so let $a = 3$ and $b = 4$: $\frac{6 + 4}{3 - 8} = \frac{10}{-5} = -2$.

questions.stem: The set $\{3, 7, 7, 10, x\}$ has a median equal to its mean. Which of the following could be the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: Whatever $x$ is, the middle value of the sorted set is 7 (two 7s sit in the middle unless $x$ moves one of them, and either way the third value is 7). So the mean must be 7: $\frac{27 + x}{5} = 7$ gives $x = 8$.

questions.passage: Riverton's city council installed speed cameras on Elm Avenue in January. In the twelve months that followed, collisions on Elm Avenue fell by 30 percent compared with the previous twelve months. The council concludes that the cameras caused the decline and plans to install cameras on five more streets.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Some drivers photographed by the cameras have disputed the fines they received.
Most collisions on Elm Avenue before January occurred during the evening rush hour.
That January a new bypass opened that cut traffic on Elm Avenue by about a third.
Speed cameras in several other cities have been criticized as a way to raise revenue.
Collisions on the five streets proposed for cameras have risen slightly in recent years.
questions.explanation: The council credits the cameras for the drop. If traffic on the avenue fell by about a third at the same time, fewer cars alone could explain 30 percent fewer collisions. The other choices do not offer another cause for the decline.

questions.passage: Kestrel Foods plans to replace its paper packaging with a new plant-based film that costs 15 percent less per unit. Kestrel's managers conclude that the switch will reduce the company's total packaging costs.
questions.stem: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Kestrel's main competitors have not yet switched to plant-based film.
Most of Kestrel's customers prefer plant-based film to the paper packaging it uses now.
The price of paper packaging is likely to rise during the coming year.
Any added costs of switching will not outweigh the saving from the lower price.
Plant-based film can be produced in the factories that now make paper.
questions.explanation: A lower price per unit lowers total cost only if switching does not bring other costs, such as new machines or more waste, that outweigh the saving; if it did, total packaging costs could rise. The other choices are not needed for the conclusion.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: describe the process by which corporate investors decide which young startups they will fund
argue that corporate venture capital usually harms the startups it funds
explain a trade-off founders face in taking corporate money
compare the financial returns of corporate and independent venture funds
recommend that founders refuse to give board seats to corporate investors
questions.explanation: The passage sets out a benefit of corporate investors (higher valuations, strategic help) against a cost (fewer rival buyers), then shows that limiting the investor trades one for the other. It does not claim the investment is harmful overall or recommend one choice.

questions.stem: According to the passage, rival buyers may hesitate to bid for a startup that has a corporate backer because
options: corporate backers usually forbid any sale of the startup to their rivals
corporate investors make startups share technical data with every buyer
the backer may know the startup's secrets or hold a right to match offers
startups with corporate backers rarely grow large enough to be acquired
the startup's valuation has been raised far above what it is really worth
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says rivals hesitate to bid for a firm whose investor 'may already know its secrets or may hold the right to match any offer.' The passage never says backers forbid sales outright.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that an independent venture fund would be least likely to
options: accept a lower financial return in exchange for early access to a technology
take a seat on the board of a startup in which it has invested
value a startup's shares at a higher price than its founders had hoped
invest in a startup that is also backed by a large corporate investor
expect its investments to return more cash than they cost within a decade
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the two kinds of investor: an independent fund succeeds only on cash returns, while a corporate arm 'often accepts a lower financial return' for a strategic benefit. Trading return for strategy is what the independent fund would least likely do.

questions.stem: The third paragraph serves mainly to
options: summarize the advantages that independent venture funds offer founders
explain why corporate investors place so much value on strategic benefits
propose a new and more reliable way to measure the cost of accepting corporate investment
describe a response to the problem raised earlier and its drawback
present evidence that contradicts the studies cited in the second paragraph
questions.explanation: The problem is that corporate backing deters rival buyers. The third paragraph gives the founders' response (limiting the investor's access) and its cost (a weaker relationship with the investor).

questions.passage: Researchers found that office workers who took a ten-minute walk after lunch made fewer errors on afternoon data-entry tasks than workers who stayed at their desks. The researchers concluded that a short walk after lunch improves afternoon concentration.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: The workers who walked said they enjoyed their lunch break more than the others.
The workers were randomly assigned either to walk or to stay at their desks.
Some of the workers who walked chose to walk with colleagues rather than alone.
Data-entry errors are more common in the afternoon than in the morning.
Many companies already encourage their employees to take short breaks.
questions.explanation: Without random assignment, workers who chose to walk might differ in ways (fitness, diligence) that explain their fewer errors. Random assignment rules that out, so the walk itself becomes the likeliest cause.

questions.passage: In Velmont, every licensed electrician must complete 16 hours of training each year. Some licensed electricians in Velmont also hold a plumbing license. No one in Velmont who holds a plumbing license is permitted to inspect gas lines.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Some licensed plumbers in Velmont complete no training of any kind each year.
Everyone who inspects gas lines in Velmont holds an electrician's license.
Most licensed electricians in Velmont also hold a plumbing license.
Some people who must train each year are not allowed to inspect gas lines.
No licensed electrician in Velmont is permitted to inspect gas lines.
questions.explanation: Some electricians hold a plumbing license. Those people must train each year (they are electricians) and may not inspect gas lines (they hold a plumbing license). So some people who must train cannot inspect gas lines. The statements say nothing about electricians without a plumbing license.

questions.passage: Sales of Brand X running shoes rose 40 percent in the year after the company hired a famous athlete to endorse them. Therefore, the endorsement deal was profitable for the company.
questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed because it
options: relies on sales figures from only a single brand of running shoes
ignores what the athlete was paid for the endorsement
treats a rise in sales as evidence that the shoes themselves are of high quality
assumes that the athlete actually wears Brand X shoes when competing
fails to consider that other brands also hire famous athletes
questions.explanation: Profitability depends on costs as well as sales. A 40 percent sales rise shows the deal was profitable only if the extra profit was larger than what the company paid the athlete, which the argument never considers.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: describing how researchers first worked out the meaning of the waggle dance
revising a view of the dance's precision and value
explaining why each individual waggle dance gives imprecise directions
comparing the foraging of honeybees with the foraging of other insects
arguing that the waggle dance matters less to honeybees than their sense of scent
questions.explanation: The passage revises the 'precise map' view in two steps: the dance matters most where food is scarce, and its value comes from averaging many noisy dances across the colony. The imprecision of single dances is one detail, not the main point.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that turning a hive on its side would most reduce the food gathered by a colony in a landscape where
options: recruits need several trips to find a food source
dancers usually orient their runs by gravity
food sources are close to the hive and plentiful
flowering plants are few and widely scattered
most foragers locate food mainly by scent
questions.explanation: Disrupted colonies 'did markedly worse' where food was 'patchy and scarce' and did almost as well where food was rich. A landscape with few, scattered flowers is the patchy, scarce case.

questions.stem: The author mentions that successive runs of a dance point in slightly different directions in order to
options: suggest that the dance signals distance but not direction
explain why disrupted colonies did well in rich landscapes
support the claim that recruits rely mainly on scent to find food
concede a weakness of single dances before explaining why it matters little
show that earlier researchers measured the angle and length of the dance in the wrong way
questions.explanation: The third paragraph admits that individual dances are noisy, then argues that a colony averages over many dancers, so the noise does not make the dance a poor signal.

questions.passage: Over the past decade, the number of public libraries in Darnell County has fallen by a quarter. Yet the total number of books borrowed from the county's libraries each year has risen.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy described above?
options: The remaining libraries now lend e-books, and those loans are counted.
The county's population has stayed about the same over the decade.
The libraries that closed were mostly in the county's smallest towns.
Many county residents now buy their books from online retailers instead of borrowing them.
Several libraries in neighboring counties have also closed in recent years.
questions.explanation: Fewer libraries but more loans is explained if each remaining library now lends far more, and adding e-book loans to the count does exactly that. Buying books online would lower loans, and the other facts do not raise them.

questions.passage: A school district plans to replace printed textbooks with tablets. The district argues that the change will save money, because each tablet costs less than the five printed textbooks that a student now uses.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the district's argument?
options: How many teachers in the district already use tablets in their classes
Whether students in the district would rather read on tablets or on printed paper
Which publisher supplies most of the district's printed textbooks
How often tablets will need repair or replacement compared with textbooks
Whether neighboring school districts have already adopted tablets
questions.explanation: The argument compares purchase prices only. If tablets break or wear out much faster than textbooks, replacing them could erase the saving, so their repair and replacement rate decides whether money is really saved.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: comparing behavioral economics with more traditional economics
tracing how thinking about a policy tool has changed
explaining why so many workers fail to save enough money for their retirement
describing the history of employer-sponsored retirement plans
arguing that employers should stop enrolling workers automatically
questions.explanation: The passage follows research on automatic enrollment from its first finding (participation rises), through a complication (people stay at the default rate), to a restated lesson about the responsibility of choosing defaults.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a drawback of early automatic enrollment plans was that
options: some workers saved at a lower rate than they would have chosen themselves
the default contribution rate rose too quickly for many workers
workers often did not realize that they had been enrolled at all
employers found the plans much more expensive to run than they had expected
many of the enrolled workers opted out soon after they were enrolled
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says enrolled workers tended to stay at the modest default rate, and 'some ended up saving less than they would have under the old system.'

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?
options: Whoever sets a default shapes the outcomes of the people who accept it.
Automatic escalation will eventually replace automatic enrollment.
Defaults help only workers who lack the time to make a choice.
The early studies of default options were poorly designed.
Workers who opt out of a retirement plan are acting against their own interests.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says defaults 'carry the designer's judgment about what people should do,' which makes choosing them a responsibility. The author does not fault the early studies; later work only added to them.

questions.passage: **Many economists predict that the new tariff on imported steel will raise costs for domestic car makers.** However, domestic steel mills currently have large unused capacity, and they have signaled that they will hold their prices steady to win market share. **Domestic car makers are therefore unlikely to face higher steel costs in the near term.**
questions.stem: In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is a prediction the argument accepts; the second is a consequence of that prediction.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is evidence offered in support of it.
The first is a prediction the argument rejects; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
The first and the second are both predictions that the argument goes on to reject.
The first is evidence that supports the second; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The argument cites the economists' prediction, then gives evidence against it (spare capacity, steady prices) and concludes, with 'therefore', that car makers are unlikely to face higher costs. So the first is rejected and the second is the conclusion.

questions.passage: Wildlife officials want to reduce collisions between cars and deer on Route 9 by building fences along the road. Critics argue that the fences will simply push deer to cross the road where the fences end. The plan is likely to reduce collisions nonetheless, since ______.
questions.stem: Which of the following most logically completes the argument?
options: deer are most active at dawn and dusk, when traffic on Route 9 is heaviest
the fences will cost less than a year of collisions between cars and deer
fences of the same design have been built along several other highways
most drivers on Route 9 are local residents who know where deer cross
the fences will end at an existing overpass that deer already use to cross
questions.explanation: The critics' worry is that deer will cross at the fences' ends. If the ends lead deer to an overpass they already use, crossings shift off the road, which answers the objection. The cost comparison does not show the plan will work.

questions.stem: The author's primary purpose is to
options: qualify a common claim about how spelling became standard
explain how compositors made each line of type reach the right margin
show that Samuel Johnson's dictionary alone fixed English spelling
argue that the early printers actively resisted efforts to standardize English spelling
describe the daily work of the earliest English printers
questions.explanation: The passage calls the claim that printing fixed spelling 'half right' and then gives the social causes that did the fixing. It qualifies the claim rather than rejecting it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, early compositors sometimes varied the spelling of a word in order to
options: save the cost of buying extra pieces of type
copy the spellings used in the manuscripts they set
make a line of type fill the full width of the page
show readers that more than one spelling was correct
follow house rules set by the large printing houses
questions.explanation: Before printers widened word spaces to fill a line, 'adding or dropping a letter was a convenient way to make each line reach the right margin.'

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about the printing press?
options: It made English spelling less consistent than scribes had made it.
It standardized English spelling within a decade of the first presses.
It made a fixed spelling possible but did not by itself produce one.
It mattered less to spelling than the word lists kept by medieval scribes.
It had little effect of any kind on how English words were spelled.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the press 'made a fixed spelling possible' but that 'the decision to fix spelling was a social one.' The author also says printers spread uniform spellings faster than scribes, so the press was not without effect.

questions.passage: To increase revenue, a museum plans to raise its admission price from \$15 to \$20. The museum's director argues that, because attendance has grown every year for the past five years, the higher price will not reduce the number of visitors enough to lower total admission revenue.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, casts the most doubt on the director's argument?
options: The museum's operating costs have risen faster than its admission revenue in recent years.
Other museums in the region charge between \$18 and \$25 for admission.
The museum has added several popular exhibitions over the past five years.
Some visitors buy annual memberships rather than paying at the door.
Most new visitors say they came mainly because the price is low.
questions.explanation: The director infers from rising attendance that visitors will not be put off by a higher price. If the recent growth came from people drawn mainly by the low price, those are the visitors most likely to stop coming, which could cut revenue.

questions.stem:
A store sold 120 shirts last month, each priced at either \$20 or \$30. How many of the shirts sold were priced at \$30?

(1) The store's revenue from the 120 shirts was \$2,900.

(2) The store sold 20 more \$20 shirts than \$30 shirts.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) If $x$ shirts sold at \$30, $30x + 20(120 - x) = 2{,}900$, so $10x = 500$ and $x = 50$: sufficient. (2) $x + (x + 20) = 120$, so $x = 50$: sufficient. Each statement alone gives 50.

questions.stem: A bakery sells muffins for \$3 each and loaves of bread for \$5 each. Yesterday it sold 50 items in all for a total of \$190. Select the number of muffins sold and the number of loaves sold.

Loaves sold

questions.stem:
Analyst: Average wait times at our call center rose this quarter even though we hired ten new agents. New agents take longer on each call while they learn, and call volume rose by a quarter after we launched a new product. So the rise in wait times does not show that the hiring was a mistake.

For each statement, select whether, if true, it would strengthen the analyst's conclusion, weaken it, or do neither.
rows: Agents hired in past years reached the team's average call time within two months.
Most of the extra calls this quarter were handled by an automated system, not by agents.
The call center moved to a larger office building last year.
The firm pays new agents the same hourly wage as experienced agents.
questions.explanation: If new agents soon reach normal speed, the slowdown is temporary and the hiring should pay off: strengthens. If agents did not handle the extra calls, the volume rise cannot explain longer waits, which leaves the hiring itself as a likelier cause: weakens. The office move and wage rates do not bear on why waits rose.

questions.stem: What is the expected first-year contribution in Market A after advertising?

Market B

questions.stem: If the retail price in Market B were raised to \$65 and expected unit sales did not change, what would the expected first-year contribution in Market B be after advertising?

questions.stem:
Set $S$ consists of the five numbers 4, 9, 13, 20 and $x$. What is the median of $S$?

Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.

EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.

questions.stem: A recipe mixes juice and soda in the ratio 3 to 5 by volume. A cook wants to make 4 liters of the mix but has only 2 liters of soda. Select the greatest amount of mix, in liters, the cook can make with the soda on hand, and the amount of juice, in liters, that this mix needs.

questions.stem:
By what percent did the price of a share of Company Q change from Monday's close to Wednesday's close?

(1) The price rose 10 percent from Monday's close to Tuesday's close.

questions.stem: If $5(x - 2) - 3(2x + 1) = -20$, what is the value of $x$?

questions.stem: If $(x - 3)^2 = 49$, what is the product of the possible values of $x$?
questions.explanation: $x - 3 = 7$ or $x - 3 = -7$, so $x = 10$ or $x = -4$. Their product is $-40$.

questions.stem: A 40-liter solution is 25 percent acid. How many liters of pure acid must be added to make a solution that is 40 percent acid?
questions.explanation: The solution has 10 liters of acid. Adding $x$ liters: $\frac{10 + x}{40 + x} = 0.4$, so $10 + x = 16 + 0.4x$, $0.6x = 6$ and $x = 10$.

questions.stem: If $2x + 3y = 13$ and $4x - y = 5$, what is the value of $x + y$?
questions.explanation: From the second equation, $y = 4x - 5$. Substitute: $2x + 12x - 15 = 13$, so $x = 2$ and $y = 3$. Then $x + y = 5$.

questions.stem: Group A has 20 students with an average score of 70. Group B has 30 students with an average score of 80. What is the average score of all 50 students?
questions.explanation: $\frac{20 \cdot 70 + 30 \cdot 80}{50} = \frac{1{,}400 + 2{,}400}{50} = 76$. It is closer to 80 because group B is larger.

questions.stem: A phone plan costs \$30 a month plus \$0.10 for each minute over 300 minutes. If a month's bill is at most \$45, what is the greatest number of minutes that could have been used?
questions.explanation: The overage is at most \$15, which buys $15 / 0.10 = 150$ extra minutes. So at most $300 + 150 = 450$ minutes.

questions.stem: Two trains start 300 miles apart and travel toward each other on parallel tracks, one at 70 miles per hour and the other at 80 miles per hour. When they pass each other, how many miles has the slower train traveled?
questions.explanation: They close the gap at $70 + 80 = 150$ miles per hour, so they meet after 2 hours. The slower train has gone $70 \cdot 2 = 140$ miles.

Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers rolled is 8?

questions.stem: Working alone, Ana takes 4 hours longer than Ben to paint a room. Working together at their usual rates, they paint the room in 3 hours and 45 minutes. How many hours does Ben take working alone?
questions.explanation: Together they take $\frac{15}{4}$ hours. If Ben takes $b$ hours, $\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{b+4} = \frac{4}{15}$. Testing the choices: $b = 6$ gives $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{10} = \frac{5 + 3}{30} = \frac{4}{15}$.

questions.stem: What is the units digit of $3^{25} \cdot 7^{10}$?
questions.explanation: Units digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1, and $25 = 4 \cdot 6 + 1$, so $3^{25}$ ends in 3. Powers of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1, and $10 = 4 \cdot 2 + 2$, so $7^{10}$ ends in 9. $3 \cdot 9 = 27$ ends in 7.

questions.stem: If $x$ is 50 percent greater than $y$ and $y$ is 20 percent less than $z$, then $x$ is what percent of $z$?
questions.explanation: $x = 1.5y$ and $y = 0.8z$, so $x = 1.5 \cdot 0.8z = 1.2z$, which is 120 percent of $z$.

questions.stem: At a firm, $\frac{2}{5}$ of the employees work remotely. Of the rest, $\frac{3}{4}$ work in the office full time, and the remaining 24 employees work a hybrid schedule. How many employees does the firm have?
questions.explanation: The non-remote share is $\frac{3}{5}$, and a quarter of it is hybrid: $\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{5} = \frac{3}{20}$ of all employees. $\frac{3}{20}E = 24$ gives $E = 160$.

questions.stem: How many integers $x$ satisfy $|2x - 3| < 7$?
Which of the following sets of numbers has the greatest standard deviation?

questions.stem: The sum of five consecutive even integers is 170. What is the greatest of the five?
questions.explanation: The middle integer is the average, $170 / 5 = 34$, so the five are 30, 32, 34, 36 and 38. The greatest is 38.

questions.stem: Which of the following fractions is greatest?
