questions.passage: In a survey, customers of Pellora Bank who use its mobile app rated their satisfaction with the bank higher than customers who do not use the app. Pellora's marketing director concludes that persuading more customers to use the app would raise customer satisfaction across the bank.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Customer satisfaction at Pellora has risen slightly over the past three years.
Pellora offers the app only to customers with no recent problems on their accounts.
Customers who use the app visit the bank's branches less often than other customers.
Some of the customers surveyed did not answer every question asked.
Many of Pellora's competitors also offer their customers mobile apps.
questions.explanation: If only customers without recent account problems may use the app, app users differ from other customers in a way that could itself explain their higher satisfaction. Getting more customers onto the app then need not raise satisfaction.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: compare the costs and benefits to firms of several different pricing strategies
argue that dynamic pricing harms the customers who pay peak prices
explain resistance to a pricing practice and how firms adapt
defend dynamic pricing against the economists who criticize it
describe how sellers decide how much new capacity to add
questions.explanation: The passage notes that economists favor dynamic pricing, explains customers' anger through reference prices and fairness, and describes how firms work around that norm.

questions.stem: According to the passage, customers are more likely to accept a price increase that
options: is announced well before it takes effect
applies to goods that the buyer needs urgently
is smaller than the increase economists predict
occurs during a period of unusually high demand
seems to reflect higher costs for the seller
questions.explanation: People 'accept increases that seem to reflect a seller's higher costs far more readily than increases that seem to exploit a buyer's urgent need.'

questions.stem: Presenting the normal price as the peak price would most likely reduce customer anger by
options: removing the need to change the price at all during a surge
persuading most customers to shift their purchases from busy periods into quiet periods
raising the prices that rival sellers charge in busy periods
lowering the costs that the seller faces during its busiest periods
making quiet-period prices seem like discounts
questions.explanation: Customers judge a price against the one they are used to. If the usual price is the high one, lower prices in quiet periods read as discounts, and a surge no longer reads as a jump above the reference point.

questions.stem: The example of the snow shovel serves mainly to
options: illustrate which price increases customers accept and which they resent
explain why some sellers add capacity when demand is high
suggest that steel prices largely determine the cost of many household goods
prove that customers judge prices by what other sellers charge
show that most sellers avoid raising their prices during storms
questions.explanation: The two shovels make the fairness norm concrete: the same higher price is resented when it exploits need after a storm and accepted when it follows a rise in costs.

questions.passage: A regional airline will add a daily flight from Corby to Lisle. Because every flight on the airline's existing Corby-Lisle route is at least 90 percent full, the airline expects the new flight to be profitable.
questions.stem: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Demand on the route is greater than the seats the current flights offer.
The new flight will use the same type of aircraft as the current flights.
Most passengers on the route travel for business rather than for leisure.
Fares on the Corby-Lisle route are higher than on the airline's other routes.
The Corby-Lisle route earns more profit than any of the airline's other routes.
questions.explanation: Full flights suggest unmet demand but do not prove it. The new flight will fill only if more people want to fly the route than the existing seats can carry; if demand just matches current capacity, the new flight would draw passengers away from the old ones.

questions.passage: In 2025, Marlow's software exports grew faster than any other category of its exports, but software still made up less than 5 percent of Marlow's total exports. Machinery exports, which make up about 40 percent of the total, grew by 2 percent.
questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
options: Software exports added more value in 2025 than machinery exports did.
Software exports grew by more than 2 percent in 2025.
Software will become Marlow's largest export within a decade.
Marlow's total exports grew by more than 2 percent in 2025.
Machinery will remain Marlow's largest category of exports.
questions.explanation: Software grew faster than every other category, including machinery, which grew 2 percent, so software must have grown by more than 2 percent. Because software is a small share, its growth in value may well be smaller than machinery's.

questions.passage: Bees foraging in fields treated with pesticide P visited fewer flowers than bees foraging in untreated fields. Scientists conclude that pesticide P impairs bees' ability to forage.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: The treated and untreated fields had the same kinds and numbers of flowers.
Bees are not the only insects that pollinate the crops in these fields.
Pesticide P is used on more farmland than any other pesticide in the region.
The scientists counted flower visits for one week in early summer.
Some farmers have stopped using pesticide P because of its rising cost.
questions.explanation: If the treated fields simply had fewer flowers, bees there would visit fewer flowers whatever the pesticide did. Showing the fields offered the same flowers removes that explanation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A detection method's built-in bias once gave a misleading picture of planets.
Astronomers should no longer rely on the transit method to find planets.
The transit method has found more planets than any other detection method.
Large planets on tight orbits are more common than astronomers once thought.
Small planets are harder for telescopes to detect than large planets are.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why the transit method favors close-orbiting planets, how that crowded early catalogs with giant close-in planets, and how corrections reversed the impression.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a planet that orbits close to its star is more likely to be found by the transit method partly because
options: it is usually larger than planets that follow wider orbits
its orbit is more likely to be aligned so that we can see it transit
it makes its star dim more deeply than a distant planet does
it reflects more of its star's light than a planet farther away does
it is less often hidden from view by the system's other planets
questions.explanation: 'The closer a planet orbits its star, the more likely that alignment is', and it also transits more often. The passage does not say close planets are larger or dim their stars more.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage primarily serves to
options: suggest that other sciences have made the same mistake
question the statistical corrections that astronomers have made
introduce a new problem with the transit method of finding planets
draw a general principle from the example the passage has discussed
restate the evidence that giant planets on tight orbits are rare
questions.explanation: After the astronomy example, the last sentence says 'the lesson extends beyond astronomy' and states it generally: understand how a sample was drawn before trusting it.

questions.passage: After a city introduced a fee on plastic shopping bags, the number of plastic bags handed out by stores fell by 80 percent. Yet sales of plastic bin liners at the same stores more than doubled.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the facts above?
options: Many residents now bring reusable cloth bags when they go shopping.
Stores are allowed to keep the money they collect from the bag fee.
The fee applies to plastic shopping bags but not to paper shopping bags.
Bin liners are usually sold in packs that last most households for several months.
Many residents once lined their bins with free store bags.
questions.explanation: If free shopping bags used to serve as bin liners, residents who stopped getting them would need to buy liners instead, so liner sales would rise as bag handouts fell.

questions.passage: Every candidate who won a seat on the city council last year spent more on advertising than her opponent did. So, to win a seat this year, a candidate needs only to outspend her opponent on advertising.
questions.stem: The argument is flawed because it
options: treats something that accompanied every win as enough to guarantee a win
ignores the fact that some candidates pay for their advertising with their own money
treats the opinions of voters as evidence about the election result
assumes that the candidates who lost will run again next year
fails to say how much the winning candidates spent on advertising
questions.explanation: Outspending the opponent went with every win, but that does not make it sufficient. Other things (incumbency, the issues, the candidate) may decide races, so outspending alone need not win a seat.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: describing the history of the Hawaiian language before the 1980s
explaining what language revival requires and where documentation fits in it
comparing the revival of Hawaiian with that of other languages
criticizing linguists for ignoring the needs of young children
arguing that the documentation of endangered languages wastes scarce resources
questions.explanation: The passage argues that revival needs children who hear a language used, illustrates this with Hawaiian immersion schools, and then shows documentation becoming essential to that effort.

questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author regards immersion schools as more effective than documentation alone at reviving a language because such schools
options: give children a setting where the language is used for real purposes
were founded by parents rather than by trained linguists
produce better grammars and dictionaries than professional linguists do
teach mathematics and science more effectively than others
need fewer fluent teachers than other kinds of schools do
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says children acquire 'languages they hear used for real purposes', and immersion schools teach the whole curriculum in the language. The passage says immersion needs more fluent teachers, not fewer.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward documentation of endangered languages is best described as
options: dismissive, because documentation seldom produces any new speakers
skeptical, because recordings of speakers are often inaccurate
neutral, because documentation serves the needs of scholars only
enthusiastic, because documentation alone can save a language
appreciative of its value once paired with teaching the language
questions.explanation: The author notes documentation rarely makes new speakers on its own but calls it 'indispensable' once immersion teaching begins, since it supplies the material for lessons.

questions.passage: Some analysts argue that the rise in home prices in Fenwick shows that the city's economy is booming. **But home prices can rise simply because few new homes are being built**, and Fenwick has issued almost no building permits in five years. Meanwhile, **the number of jobs in Fenwick has fallen for three straight years**. The rise in home prices is therefore poor evidence of a booming economy.
questions.stem: In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence the analysts cite; the second is evidence the argument cites against them.
The first offers another explanation for an observation; the second is evidence for the main conclusion.
The first is a claim the argument rejects; the second is a claim that the argument accepts.
The first is the argument's main conclusion; the second is evidence that supports that conclusion.
The first offers another explanation for an observation; the second is the argument's main conclusion.
questions.explanation: The analysts read rising prices as a booming economy. The first portion offers another reason prices can rise (few new homes). The second, falling jobs, is evidence for the conclusion stated in the last sentence, that rising prices are poor evidence of a boom.

questions.passage: A hospital plans to reduce patient falls by installing bed alarms that alert nurses when a high-risk patient gets out of bed. Hospital managers predict that, once the alarms are installed, the number of falls will drop sharply.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the managers' prediction?
options: Whether patients' families have asked the hospital for bed alarms
How many of the hospital's beds are in private rooms
How much the bed alarms cost compared with other kinds of patient safety equipment
Whether nurses can reach a room within seconds of an alarm
Whether the alarm maker also produces other medical devices
questions.explanation: An alarm prevents a fall only if a nurse arrives before the patient falls. If nurses usually cannot get there in time, the alarms will do little; if they can, the prediction is more plausible.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: explain why Renoir preferred certain new pigments to others
argue that the Impressionists painted mainly in their studios rather than outdoors
revise a common account of how a technology influenced an art movement
describe how painters stored their paint before the 1840s
show that the paint tube had little effect on painting
questions.explanation: The passage doubts the usual story (the tube made outdoor painting possible) and replaces it with a less obvious one (the tube brought ready-mixed bright pigments).

questions.stem: The author mentions that painters had sketched outdoors in oils long before the tube in order to
options: support Renoir's remark about the importance of the tube
show that the Impressionists learned their methods from earlier painters
cast doubt on the claim that the tube made outdoor painting possible
explain why painters stored their paint in pig bladders
suggest that outdoor sketches were valued less than studio work
questions.explanation: The fact follows 'Such remarks deserve some skepticism': if painters worked outdoors before the tube existed, the tube cannot be what made outdoor work possible.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the paint tube contributed to the Impressionists' bright palette by
options: making intense new ready-mixed pigments easy for painters to use
letting painters blend their colors directly on the canvas
keeping pigments from fading after they had been applied
allowing painters to work outdoors in the brightest sunlight
lowering the price of pigments such as synthetic ultramarine
questions.explanation: Tube makers sold new, intense pigments ready-mixed, so painters could lay bright colors directly on the canvas 'without first grinding and mixing them.'

questions.passage: To reduce traffic congestion, the city of Lanport will charge drivers \$8 to enter the city center on weekdays. City planners predict that, as a result, weekday traffic in the city center will fall by about 20 percent.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the planners' prediction?
options: Traffic downtown is much lighter on weekends than it is on weekdays.
Lanport plans to spend the money raised by the charge on improving its bus service.
Some downtown shop owners worry that the charge will reduce their number of customers.
Similar charges in other cities were unpopular when they were first introduced.
Most weekday drivers downtown have their tolls paid by employers.
questions.explanation: A charge cuts traffic by making driving cost more. If most drivers' employers pay it for them, the drivers feel no added cost and have little reason to stop driving downtown.

questions.passage: Grovetech will move its call center from a city where it pays workers \$22 an hour to a town where comparable workers earn \$16 an hour. Grovetech's managers conclude that the move will lower the call center's operating costs.
questions.stem: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Workers in the town are as happy in their jobs as workers in the city are.
The town has offered Grovetech a tax break to open the call center there.
Grovetech's competitors pay their call center staff more than \$16 an hour.
Savings on wages will not be offset by higher costs for training, travel or rent.
Most of Grovetech's customers live much closer to the town than they do to the city.
questions.explanation: Lower wages cut total operating costs only if other costs do not rise by more. If the move brought much higher training, travel or rent costs, operating costs could go up despite the wage saving.

questions.stem:
What is the value of $x + y$?

(1) $2x + 2y = 18$

(2) $x - y = 3$
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) Divide by 2: $x + y = 9$: sufficient. (2) Gives only the difference; $x = 5, y = 2$ and $x = 4, y = 1$ both work: not sufficient.

questions.passage:
**Five hotels on an average night**

| Hotel | Rooms | Occupancy | Average nightly rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Harbor | 120 | 85% | \$180 |
| Summit | 200 | 70% | \$150 |
| Meadow | 80 | 90% | \$220 |
| Station | 150 | 78% | \$140 |
| Garden | 100 | 82% | \$195 |
questions.stem: For each statement, select True if it is supported by the information in the table. Otherwise select False.
rows: The hotel with the most rooms also has the most occupied rooms on an average night.
Meadow earns more room revenue on an average night than Harbor does.
Across the five hotels, more than 80 percent of all rooms are occupied on an average night.
questions.explanation: Occupied rooms: Harbor 102, Summit 140, Meadow 72, Station 117, Garden 82, so Summit, with the most rooms, also has the most occupied: true. Revenue: Meadow $72 \times 220 = 15{,}840$; Harbor $102 \times 180 = 18{,}360$: false. Occupied rooms total 513 of 650, about 78.9 percent: false.

questions.passage:
**Line graph: annual revenue of a software firm (\$ millions)**

| Year | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | 40 | 46 | 50 | 48 | 57 |
questions.stem: Revenue grew by about [[1]] from 2024 to 2025, and revenue fell in [[2]] of the four year-to-year changes shown.
questions.explanation: From 48 to 57 is a rise of 9 on a base of 48: $9 / 48 \approx 18.75$ percent, about 19 percent. Revenue fell only from 2023 to 2024 (50 to 48): one change.

questions.stem: An investor puts a total of \$12,000 into two funds, one earning 5 percent a year and the other 8 percent a year. After one year the investments have earned \$816 in total. Select the amount invested in each fund.
rows: Amount in the 5 percent fund
Amount in the 8 percent fund

questions.stem:
If $k$ is an integer, is $k$ odd?

(1) $k^2 + k$ is even.

(2) $3k + 1$ is even.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) $k^2 + k = k(k + 1)$ is a product of consecutive integers, so it is even for every $k$: not sufficient. (2) $3k$ must be odd, so $k$ is odd: sufficient.

questions.stem: The median score falls in the [[1]] group, and [[2]] percent of the applicants scored 80 or higher.
questions.explanation: With 50 scores the median is between the 25th and 26th. The running totals are 4, 13 and 30, so both fall in 70-79. Scores of 80 or more: $14 + 6 = 20$ of 50, which is 40 percent.

questions.stem:
Firm F has 80 employees. How many of them speak both French and German?

(1) 30 of the employees speak French and 25 speak German.

(2) 35 of the employees speak neither French nor German.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) Anywhere from 0 to 25 could speak both: not sufficient. (2) 45 speak at least one language, but the split is unknown: not sufficient. Together: $30 + 25 - \text{both} = 45$, so 10 speak both: sufficient.

questions.stem: For each candidate, select whether the candidate is invited to a second interview.
rows: Ruiz
Patel
Okafor
Nguyen
questions.explanation: Ruiz meets all three requirements. Patel has only 2 years of supervisory experience. Okafor's scheduled forklift exam counts as meeting the requirement, and Okafor meets the other two. Nguyen is not available for night shifts.

questions.stem: Which candidate will be ranked first among those invited to a second interview?
options: Nguyen
Brandt
Okafor
Patel
Ruiz
questions.explanation: The invited candidates are Ruiz, Okafor and Brandt. Only Brandt has the preferred logistics degree, so Brandt ranks first even though Ruiz has more experience. Patel and Nguyen are not invited.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if it happened, would increase the number of candidates invited to a second interview?
options: Ruiz completes a degree in logistics.
Okafor's forklift exam is moved past the start date.
Brandt withdraws from consideration.
Patel passes a second forklift exam.
Nguyen becomes available for night shifts.
questions.explanation: Nguyen meets every requirement except night availability, so becoming available would make Nguyen a fourth invitee. A degree changes ranking, not invitations; Patel still lacks experience; moving Okafor's exam or Brandt withdrawing would reduce the number.

questions.stem: A cyclist rides 30 kilometers to a town and returns by the same road. The trip out takes 1.5 hours, and the return trip, against the wind, takes 2 hours. Select the cyclist's average speed for the round trip and the cyclist's speed on the return trip, both in kilometers per hour.
rows: Average speed for the round trip
Speed on the return trip
questions.explanation: The round trip is 60 kilometers in 3.5 hours: $60 / 3.5 \approx 17.1$. The return is 30 kilometers in 2 hours: 15. Averaging the two speeds, 20 and 15, to get 17.5 ignores that more time was spent at the slower speed.

questions.stem:
If $a$ and $b$ are positive, is $\frac{a}{b} > 1$?

(1) $a - b > 0$

(2) $a^2 > b^2$
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Because $b > 0$, $\frac{a}{b} > 1$ exactly when $a > b$. (1) says $a > b$: sufficient. (2) For positive numbers, $a^2 > b^2$ means $a > b$: sufficient.

questions.passage:
**End-of-term results in five courses**

| Course | Students | Passed | Average score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accounting | 64 | 48 | 71 |
| Biology | 80 | 52 | 68 |
| Chemistry | 45 | 36 | 74 |
| Design | 30 | 27 | 82 |
| Economics | 72 | 54 | 70 |
questions.stem: For each statement, select True if it is supported by the information in the table. Otherwise select False.
rows: Two of the courses had the same pass rate.
The course with the highest average score also had the highest pass rate.
More than 75 percent of all the students in the five courses passed.
questions.explanation: Pass rates: Accounting 48/64 = 75%, Biology 52/80 = 65%, Chemistry 36/45 = 80%, Design 27/30 = 90%, Economics 54/72 = 75%. Accounting and Economics match: true. Design has both the highest average (82) and the highest pass rate: true. In all, 217 of 291 students passed, about 74.6 percent: false.

questions.passage:
**Line graph: weekly output of two plants (units)**

Two straight lines start at week 0. Plant A starts at 500 units and rises by 40 units each week. Plant B starts at 800 units and falls by 20 units each week.
questions.stem: Plant A's weekly output first exceeds Plant B's in week [[1]], when Plant A produces [[2]] more units than Plant B.
questions.explanation: Plant A makes $500 + 40w$ and Plant B $800 - 20w$ in week $w$. They are equal when $60w = 300$, at week 5, so A first exceeds B in week 6: $740 - 680 = 60$ units.

questions.stem:
A jar contains only red marbles and green marbles. If one marble is chosen at random, what is the probability that it is red?

(1) There are 24 marbles in the jar.

(2) The ratio of red marbles to green marbles is 1 to 3.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: (1) The total alone says nothing about the colors: not sufficient. (2) Red is 1 of every 4 marbles, so the probability is $\frac{1}{4}$: sufficient.

questions.stem:
To encourage people to ride its new light-rail line, a city plans to remove 20 percent of the parking spaces downtown. City planners say the change will not hurt downtown shops.

For each statement, select whether, if true, it would strengthen the planners' claim, weaken it, or do neither.
rows: Most downtown shoppers live in areas that the rail line does not serve.
Downtown parking meters were last replaced ten years ago.
Since the line opened, downtown sales to rail riders have grown faster than total downtown sales.
The rail line was built with federal as well as city funds.
questions.explanation: If most shoppers cannot use the rail line, losing parking may keep them away: weakens. Growing sales to rail riders show shops gaining customers who do not need parking: strengthens. The age of the parking meters and the line's funding do not bear on shop sales.

questions.stem: For each statement, select True if it is supported by the information in the table. Otherwise select False.
rows: The route with the most stops has the highest fuel use per 100 kilometers.
The route with the fewest stops uses the least fuel in total.
R2 uses more fuel per kilometer than R5 does.
questions.explanation: Fuel per 100 km: R1 12, R2 14, R3 10, R4 16, R5 13. R4 has the most stops (30) and the highest rate: true. R3 has the fewest stops but uses 15.0 liters, more than R4's 9.6: false. R2 uses 0.14 liter per km against R5's 0.13: true.

questions.stem:
What was Ana's average speed, in miles per hour, for her 120-mile trip?

(1) She drove the first 60 miles at 40 miles per hour.

(2) She drove the last 60 miles in 1 hour.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time. (1) gives the first 1.5 hours only; (2) gives the last hour only: neither is sufficient. Together the trip took 2.5 hours, so $120 / 2.5 = 48$: sufficient.

questions.passage:
**Stacked bar chart: smartphone shipments by brand (millions)**

| Year | Brand X | Brand Y | Brand Z | Others | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 30 | 25 | 15 | 30 | 100 |
| 2025 | 33 | 22 | 21 | 34 | 110 |
questions.stem: Brand Z's market share rose by about [[1]] percentage points from 2024 to 2025, and the group whose shipments grew by the largest percent was [[2]].
questions.explanation: Brand Z's share went from $15 / 100 = 15$ percent to $21 / 110 \approx 19.1$ percent, a rise of about 4 points (6 is the change in units, 40 the percent growth). Growth: X 10%, Y -12%, Z 40%, Others about 13%.

questions.stem:
If $n$ is a positive integer, is $n$ divisible by 8?

(1) $n$ is divisible by 4.

(2) $n$ is divisible by 6.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
questions.explanation: Together, $n$ is a multiple of 12. 12 is not divisible by 8, but 24 is: not sufficient. Each statement alone allows both answers too.

questions.stem: What is 0.6 percent of 450?
questions.explanation: 0.6 percent is $0.006$, and $0.006 \cdot 450 = 2.7$. Answering 270 treats 0.6 percent as 0.6.

questions.stem: If $x^2 - y^2 = 48$ and $x + y = 12$, what is the value of $x$?
questions.explanation: $x^2 - y^2 = (x + y)(x - y)$, so $x - y = 4$. Adding $x + y = 12$ gives $2x = 16$ and $x = 8$.

questions.stem: Bus A leaves a station every 12 minutes and bus B every 18 minutes. Both leave at 8:00 a.m. At what time do they next leave together?
questions.explanation: They leave together every $\text{lcm}(12, 18) = 36$ minutes, so next at 8:36 a.m.

questions.stem: If $\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{4}$ and $xy = 48$, what is the value of $x + y$?
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} = \frac{x + y}{xy}$, so $\frac{x + y}{48} = \frac{1}{4}$ and $x + y = 12$.

questions.stem: A coat lists for \$80. It is discounted 15 percent, and then 8 percent sales tax is added to the discounted price. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: Discounted price: $80 \cdot 0.85 = 68$. With tax: $68 \cdot 1.08 = 73.44$.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes every value of $x$ for which $x^2 < 4x$?
questions.explanation: $x^2 - 4x < 0$ means $x(x - 4) < 0$, which holds when the factors have opposite signs: $0 < x < 4$. Test $x = 2$: $4 < 8$, true.

questions.stem: What is the greatest prime factor of $3^8 - 1$?
questions.explanation: $3^8 - 1 = (3^4 - 1)(3^4 + 1) = 80 \cdot 82 = 2^5 \cdot 5 \cdot 41$. The greatest prime factor is 41; 82 is $2 \cdot 41$, not a prime.

questions.stem: A town's population doubles every 6 years. If the population is 5,000 now, in how many years will it be 40,000?
questions.explanation: 40,000 is $8 = 2^3$ times 5,000, so three doublings are needed: $3 \cdot 6 = 18$ years.

questions.stem: The probability of rain on Saturday is 0.4 and on Sunday is 0.3, and the two events are independent. What is the probability that it rains on at least one of the two days?
questions.explanation: The chance of no rain on either day is $0.6 \cdot 0.7 = 0.42$, so the chance of rain on at least one day is $1 - 0.42 = 0.58$. Adding 0.4 and 0.3 counts rain on both days twice.

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = x^2 + bx + c$ has zeros at $x = 2$ and $x = -5$. What is the value of $f(0)$?
What is the median of the first 20 positive multiples of 3?
questions.explanation: The multiples run 3, 6, ..., 60. With 20 values the median is the average of the 10th and 11th, 30 and 33, which is 31.5.

questions.stem: A tank holds 300 liters of water. It is drained at 12 liters per minute while it is filled at 8 liters per minute. After how many minutes will it hold 180 liters?
questions.explanation: The net loss is $12 - 8 = 4$ liters a minute. Losing $300 - 180 = 120$ liters takes $120 / 4 = 30$ minutes.

questions.passage: A study found that people who drink green tea every day have lower rates of heart disease than people who do not. A tea company concludes that drinking green tea protects against heart disease.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: Green tea contains less caffeine per cup than coffee or than most black teas do.
Some people in the study drank several cups of green tea every day.
The tea company sells green tea along with several kinds of black tea.
People who drink green tea daily also tend to exercise more and smoke less.
Heart disease is much more common in older people than in younger people.
questions.explanation: If green-tea drinkers also exercise more and smoke less, those habits could explain their lower heart disease rates, so the tea need not be the cause.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: compare the ride-hailing business with the messaging business
explain why online platforms become more valuable to each of their users as they grow
argue that network effects protect leaders only in some conditions
show that winner-take-all markets have never existed among platforms
describe how several early social networks lost their lead
questions.explanation: The passage tests the claim that network effects make a leader unassailable, shows leaders have fallen, and names the conditions (multihoming, locality) that decide whether the effect protects a leader.

questions.stem: The passage describes multihoming as a situation in which
options: a single platform operates in several different cities at once
a market leader buys the platforms that compete with it
buyers and sellers both use the same platform to trade
users take part in more than one competing platform at the same time
a newcomer copies the most popular features of a market leader
questions.explanation: Multihoming is when 'users can easily use several platforms at once, as many drivers and riders do with competing ride-hailing apps.'

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a newcomer would find it hardest to challenge a leading platform that
options: charges its users more than its main rivals charge them
operates only within individual cities rather than nationally
links users worldwide and that users seldom use alongside a rival
has lost a large number of users to its rivals in the past
lets its drivers also work for competing ride-hailing apps
questions.explanation: Both features that let newcomers in are absent here: no multihoming (users seldom use a rival too) and no locality (the network's value is worldwide, so there is no city to win first).

questions.stem: The examples of early social networks and online auction sites are mentioned in order to
options: challenge the view that a platform's lead cannot be overcome
explain why network effects raise the cost of entry
show that local networks are easier for newcomers to enter
illustrate how multihoming works in practice for users
suggest that platforms are less valuable than they appear
questions.explanation: They follow 'The history of such markets is less tidy' as cases of once-dominant platforms that lost their lead, which contradicts the winner-take-all claim.

questions.passage: New software lets each claims processor at Brentwood Insurance handle 30 percent more claims per day. Brentwood's managers conclude that the company will be able to process its claims with fewer staff.
questions.stem: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Brentwood's claim volume will not rise sharply after the change.
The new software costs less each year than hiring and training new claims processors.
Most of the claims Brentwood receives are for automobile insurance.
Claims processors at Brentwood prefer the new software to the old system.
Several of Brentwood's competitors already use similar claims software.
questions.explanation: Faster processing means fewer staff are needed only for the same volume of claims. If claims rose by as much as productivity, Brentwood would still need its current staff.

questions.passage: Every vehicle in Sanford's delivery fleet is either electric or hybrid. None of the fleet's hybrid vehicles has a range of more than 500 miles. Some of the fleet's vehicles have a range of more than 500 miles.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Some of the fleet's electric vehicles have a range of more than 500 miles.
None of the fleet's electric vehicles has a range of under 500 miles.
Every electric vehicle sold in Sanford has a range over 500 miles.
The fleet has more electric vehicles than it has hybrid vehicles.
Most of the vehicles in Sanford's delivery fleet are electric rather than hybrid.
questions.explanation: Some fleet vehicles go more than 500 miles, and no hybrid does, so those vehicles must be electric. Nothing tells us how many electric vehicles there are or the range of the others.

questions.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with

comparing several coral species that differ in their heat tolerance
proposing experiments that could raise the heat tolerance of corals

questions.passage: Over the past five years, the price of solar panels has fallen sharply. Yet the share of homes in Pellham with rooftop solar panels has barely changed.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the facts above?
options: Pellham gets more sunshine each year than most towns in the region.
Homes in nearby towns have added solar panels at a faster rate.
Solar panels now turn more sunlight into electricity than they did before.
Labor and permit fees, which are most of a home system's cost, have risen.
Most Pellham homes with solar panels installed them over five years ago.

questions.passage: A grocery chain added self-checkout lanes to half of its stores. A year later, the average customer waiting time in those stores had fallen by 40 percent, while in the chain's other stores it was unchanged. The chain concludes that the self-checkout lanes reduced waiting times.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
options: Waiting times in grocery stores are longest on weekend afternoons.
Self-checkout lanes cost less to operate than staffed checkout lanes.
The chain plans to add self-checkout lanes to its remaining stores next year.
Before the change, both store groups had similar traffic and waits.
Some customers say that they strongly prefer staffed checkout lanes to self-checkout lanes.
questions.explanation: The comparison is persuasive only if the two groups of stores were alike to begin with. Showing similar traffic and waits before the change makes the self-checkout lanes the likeliest cause of the difference.
